Empirical Research Plan ­– “Chinese Import Competition and U.S. Local Labor Markets”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Chosen design: Shift-share two–stage least squares (SS-2SLS) implemented in a panel difference-in-differences framework.

Why appropriate
•  Treatment intensity varies continuously across 722 commuting zones (CZs) according to their pre-1990 industry mix.  
•  The shift (national/​international Chinese export growth by industry) is plausibly exogenous to individual CZ shocks once it is purged of U.S. demand by using exports to other high-income countries.  
•  Panel data (1990, 2000, 2007) allow us to difference out time-invariant CZ factors and common macro shocks with CZ and year fixed effects.

Specification (conceptual):
1st stage:  ΔIPW_it = π · Z_it + γ_i + θ_t + ε_it   
 Z_it = Σ_j s_ij,1990 · ΔX_OCjt / L_jt           (shift-share instrument)  
2nd stage:  Y_it = β · ĤΔIPW_it + γ_i + θ_t + X_it′ δ + u_it  

where Y_it is manufacturing employment rate, log wages, or transfer payments per capita in CZ i at time t.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control Definitions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable
•  ΔIPW_it  = annualised change in Chinese imports per U.S. worker allocated to CZ i:
 ΔIPW_it = Σ_j (L_ij,1990 / L_i,1990) · (ΔM_UCjt / L_jt)

Control group
•  CZs with low (near-zero) predicted exposure serve as the counterfactual; every CZ enters the regression, so the design is “dose–response” rather than binary treatment.

Timing
•  Two periods: 1990-2000 (“pre-WTO accession build-up”) and 2000-2007 (“post-accession surge”). We estimate stacked first-differences (1990–2000, 2000–2007) and treat each ten-year change as an observation.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Quasi-random exposure: Conditional on 1990 industry shares, Chinese export growth to other high-income countries (the instrument) is orthogonal to idiosyncratic CZ labour-demand shocks.  
Plausibility: Chinese productivity shocks or WTO-related policy changes are supply-side and common across destination markets.

A2. Relevance: Chinese exports to other wealthy countries are strongly correlated with Chinese exports to the U.S. (first-stage F-stat≫10).  
Supported by data: Cross-industry correlation is ~0.8 over 1990-2007.

A3. Parallel trends (for validity of the shift-share DiD component): Absent the China shock, high- and low-exposure CZs would have followed similar trends.  
Plausibility: Testable in pre-period (1980-1990) using retrospective employment data.

A4. No significant labour-market spillovers across CZs (SUTVA).  
Plausibility: Some migration and input-output linkages exist; will be probed with robustness checks using placebo services employment.

A5. Stable shares assumption: 1990 industry employment shares are predetermined with respect to post-1990 China shock.  
Plausibility: 1990 predates the large export surge; industry composition inertia is high.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Common demand shocks across high-income countries (violating exclusion).  
 Fix:  Control for contemporaneous industry-specific global demand using world (ex-China) import growth; include destination-year fixed effects.  Sensitivity: instrument on a leave-one-out basis (drop each destination in turn).

T2. Selective migration or re-sorting of workers across CZs.  
 Fix:  Estimate outcomes for non-migrants (individuals living in same CZ five years earlier, observable in Census long-form/ACS); instrument for ΔIPW_it in population-weighted or fixed-population samples.

T3. Heterogeneous pre-trends.  
 Fix:  Include CZ-specific linear trends; show pre-1990 placebo coefficients are near zero; conduct event-study graph (1980, 1990, 2000, 2007).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ---- 0. Packages ----
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(ivpack)   # for weak-IV diagnostics
library(ggplot2)

# ---- 1. Load data ----
cbp  <- fread("cbp_cz_industry_1990_2000_2007.csv")   # L_ijt, L_it
trade_us  <- fread("china_us_imports_by_industry.csv")   # ΔM_UCj
trade_oth <- fread("china_exports_other8_by_industry.csv") # instrument
bls  <- fread("cz_wages_1990_2000_2007.csv")
ssa  <- fread("cz_transfers_1990_2000_2007.csv")

# ---- 2. Construct Shift-Share Variables ----
# 2a. 1990 employment shares
cbp_1990 <- cbp[year==1990, .(s_ij = employment / sum(employment)), by=.(cz, industry)]

# 2b. Industry-level import changes
trade_us[, dM_uc := value / lag(value), by = industry]
trade_oth[, dX_oth := value / lag(value), by = industry]

# Collapse to 10-year changes (1990-2000, 2000-2007)
change_us  <- trade_us[year %in% c(1990,2000,2007)]
change_oth <- trade_oth[year %in% c(1990,2000,2007)]

# 2c. Merge and compute predicted exposure for each CZ-period
exposure_dt <- CJ(cz = unique(cbp$cz),
                  year = c(2000,2007))  # end-years of intervals

make_exposure <- function(endyear){
  baseyear <- ifelse(endyear==2000,1990,2000)
  shares <- cbp[year==baseyear,.(cz, industry, share = employment/sum(employment)),by=cz]
  shifts <- change_us[year==endyear,.(industry, shift = dM_uc)]
  ex <- merge(shares, shifts, by="industry")
  ex[, exposure := share * shift]
  out <- ex[,.(IPW = sum(exposure)), by=cz]
  out[, year := endyear]
}

IPW <- rbindlist(lapply(c(2000,2007), make_exposure))

# Instrument: replace dM_uc with dX_oth
make_instr <- function(endyear){
  baseyear <- ifelse(endyear==2000,1990,2000)
  shares <- cbp[year==baseyear,.(cz, industry, share = employment/sum(employment)),by=cz]
  shifts <- change_oth[year==endyear,.(industry, shift = dX_oth)]
  ex <- merge(shares, shifts, by="industry")
  ex[, exposure_z := share * shift]
  out <- ex[,.(Z = sum(exposure_z)), by=cz]
  out[, year := endyear]
}
Z <- rbindlist(lapply(c(2000,2007), make_instr))

# ---- 3. Outcome Variables ----
outcomes <- merge(bls, ssa, by=c("cz","year"), all=TRUE) # wages, transfers
panel <- Reduce(function(x,y) merge(x,y,by=c("cz","year"),all=TRUE),
                list(IPW, Z, outcomes))
panel[, period := ifelse(year==2000, "1990_2000", "2000_2007")]

# ---- 4. Main 2SLS Regression ----
# Example: effect on manufacturing employment rate
est <- feols(manu_emp_rate ~ 1 | cz + period ~ IPW | Z, data=panel, cluster="cz")
summary(est)

# ---- 5. Robustness: CZ-specific trends ----
panel[, tnum := ifelse(year==2000,0,1)]   # dummy for second window
est_trend <- feols(manu_emp_rate ~ tnum | cz + period + cz:tnum ~ IPW | Z,
                   data=panel, cluster="cz")
summary(est_trend)

# Weak-IV test
ivdiagnostics(est)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Direction: Higher exposure to Chinese imports lowers manufacturing employment and wages and raises transfer payments.

Magnitude (based on theory and past evidence): A $1,000 (2007$) increase in annual Chinese imports per worker is expected to reduce the manufacturing employment rate in a CZ by roughly 0.8–1.0 percentage points and lower average manufacturing wages by 1–2%. Disability and retirement transfer receipts likely rise by 5–10 dollars per capita.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV / shift-share)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1. Instrument relevance (first-stage F-stat > 10) ………………… 1  
C2. Exclusion: instrument uncorrelated with CZ demand shocks …… 0.5  
C3. Common trends / no differential pre-trends …………………… 0.8  
C4. No treatment spillovers across CZs (SUTVA) …………………… 0.7  
C5. Correct inference (clustered SE, robust specs) ………………… 1  

Total: 4.0 / 5 – Overall credible but some residual concerns about exclusion and spillovers.
